source_text: ἐστιν ἢ καταδέξασθαι ἢ παραιτήσασθαι τὸ πάθος. Εἰ δὲ οὐκ ἐν σοὶ κεῖται, εἰκότως δειλιᾷς ὡς ἄκων καὶ παρὰ γνώμην ἐπὶ τὸ πάθος ἑλκόμενος. Εἰ δὲ ἄκων τὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν θάνατον ἀναδέχῃ, πῶς λέγεις· Ἐξουσίαν ἔχω θεῖναι τὴν ψυχήν μου καὶ ἐξουσίαν ἔχω πάλιν τοῦ λαβεῖν αὐτήν, πῶς δὲ πάλιν ἐν ἑτέρῳ χωρίῳ παίζων τῶν Ἰουδαίων τὴν ἀπειλὴν ἔλεγες· Λύσατε τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον καὶ ἐν τρισὶν ἡμέραις ἐγερῶ αὐτόν; Ὁ τοίνυν πολλαχῶς πολλάκις πρὸ τοῦ θανάτου τὸν θάνατον προτυπώσας καὶ πρὸ τοῦ σταυροῦ τὸ τοῦ σταυροῦ τρόπαιον διαγράψας, ὁ εἰπὼν ὅτι δεῖ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου παραδοθῆναι καὶ σταυρωθῆναι καὶ ταφῆναι καὶ τῇ τρίτῃ ἡμέρᾳ ἀναστῆναι, τί ἐλθὼν νῦν ὑπὸ τὸν σταυρὸν τὸν θάνατον παραιτῇ; Εἰ γὰρ δεῖ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου παραδοθῆ ναι, πῶς λέγεις· Εἰ δυνατὸν παρελθάτω τὸ ποτήριον τοῦτο; Ὅλως δὲ εἰ τὸ μὴ παθεῖν ἐβούλου, τί τὸ παθητὸν ἐνεδύου σῶμα; Εἰ δὲ σῶμα παθητὸν φορέσας ἐπὶ τὸ πάθος ἔρχῃ, τί λυπῇ καὶ δυσχεραί νεις; Πῶς δὲ ὅτε τὸν θάνατον διέγραφες, ὅτε τὸ πάθος ἱστόρεις, ὅτε τὸν σταυρὸν προετύπους, πρὸς Πέτρον ἠγανάκτεις λέγοντα· Ἵλεώς σοι, κύριε, οὐ μὴ ἔσται σοι τοῦτο καὶ οὕτως ἠγανάκτεις ὡς λέγειν· Ὕπαγε ὀπίσω μου, σατανᾶ, σκάνδαλόν μου εἶ, ὅτι οὐ φρονεῖς τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀλλὰ τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων; Εἰ οὖν ἀνθρώπινόν ἐστιν φρόνημα, τὸ τὸν θάνατον παραιτεῖσθαι, τίνος ἕνεκεν νῦν ἐπιζη τεῖς ὃ πάλαι διεκώλυες; Πῶς δὲ νῦν ἐκκλῖναι τὸν θάνατον εὔχῃ, ὁ πάλαι τῷ μαθητῇ ἐπιτιμῶν διὰ τὸ δειλιᾶν τοῦ θανάτου τὴν προσβολήν; Οὐ σὺ εἶ ὑπὸ τοῦ νόμου καὶ τῶν προφητῶν προ αναφωνούμενος; Οὐ περὶ σοῦ Ὠσηὲ ὁ προφήτης ἔλεγεν· Τάδε λέγει κύριος· Ἐκ χειρὸς ᾅδου ῥύσομαι αὐτούς, ἵνα εἴπωσιν· Ποῦ ἡ νίκη σου, θάνατε, ποῦ τὸ κέντρον σου, ᾅδη; Εἰ οὖν σὺ εἶ ὁ ἐκ τοῦ ᾅδου ῥυόμενος, πῶς δειλιᾷς τὸν θάνατον; Εἰ δὲ σὺ τὸν θάνατον δειλιᾷς, δι' οὗ τὸν θάνατον νικᾶν ἐλπίζομεν, ματαία ἡμῶν ἡ ἐλπίς, ἀνόνητος ἡ προσδοκία. Ὅλως δὲ εἰ σὺ τὸν θάνατον φοβῇ, ἐν τίνι ἕξομεν λοιπὸν τὰς τῆς ζωῆς ἐλπίδας, πῶς δὲ λέγεις· Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ζωὴ καὶ ἡ ἀνάστασις; Ζωὴ γὰρ θάνατον οὐ φοβεῖται, ἀνάστασις πάθος οὐ δειλιᾷ. Ἀλλὰ σὺ εἶ ἡ ζωὴ καὶ ἡ ἀνάστασις. Τί μου οὖν φοβεῖς τὴν ψυχήν, τί μου τοὺς τόνους τῆς διανοίας ἐκλύεις δειλίας προ φέρων ῥήματα; Μὴ φάσμα ἦν τὰ κατὰ τὸν Λάζαρον; Μὴ ὄναρ ἦν τὰ κατὰ τὴν Ἰαείρου θυγατέρα; Μὴ σκιὰ ἦν τὰ κατὰ τὸν υἱὸν τῆς χήρας; Ἀλλὰ ἀλήθεια ἦν τὰ γεγενημένα. Πῶς οὖν ὁ τὸν θάνατον σκυλεύσας θάνατον φοβῇ, πῶς δὲ ὁ τοὺς νεκροὺς ὀδωδότας μετ' ἐξουσίας ἐγείρων εὔχῃ καὶ δειλιᾷς τῷ θανάτῳ μὴ περιπε σεῖν; Τί δὲ ὅλως τὸ περιπεσεῖν φοβῇ; Κἂν γὰρ περιπέσῃς, ἐλευθερώσῃ. Ὁ γὰρ ἑτέρους ἀνιστῶν, πολλῷ μᾶλλον τὸ ἑαυτοῦ ἐγείρει σῶμα. Ἢ φράσον οὖν μοι τὴν ἔννοιαν, δέσποτα, ἢ παῦσαι τοῦ ῥήματος καὶ μὴ διέλῃς μου τὴν ψυχήν, ἢ ὀκλᾶσαι ποιήσῃς τὸν λογισμόν. Εἰ γὰρ σὺ εἶ ὁ πάντα εἰδὼς πρὶν γενέσεως αὐτῶν, πῶς νῦν ἀγνοεῖς πότερον δυνατόν ἐστιν ἢ ἀδύνατον παρελθεῖν τὸ ποτήριον; Εἰ μὲν γὰρ ἀγνοεῖς, ψεύδεται Παῦλος λέγων ὅτι Οὐκ ἔστι κτίσις ἀφανὴς ἐνώπιόν σου, πάντα δὲ γυμνὰ καὶ τετραχηλισμένα τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς αὐτοῦ. Εἰ δὲ γινώσκεις, πῶς λέγεις· Εἰ δυνατόν; Ἀγνοοῦντός ἐστι πεῦσις καὶ οὐκ εἰδότος ἀπόφασις. Φράσον οὖν ἡμῖν, δέσποτα, τῶν εἰρημένων τὴν ἔννοιαν. Νῦν γὰρ Εὐνόμιος χαίρει, νῦν Ἄρειος εὐφραίνεται εἰς ὑπόθεσιν βλασφημίας τὸν λόγον ἁρπάζοντες. Ἀλλὰ μάτην χαίρονται. Οὐ γὰρ ἔστι χαίρειν τοῖς ἀσεβέσι, λέγει κύριος. Οὐ φοβοῦμαι γὰρ τὸν θάνατον, ὥς φασιν· οὐ παραιτοῦμαι τὸ πάθος, ὡς νομίζουσιν. 2 Εἰ γὰρ μὴ ἤθελον διὰ θανάτου ζωὴν χαρίσασθαι τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων, οὐκ ἄν, λόγος ὢν ἀπαθής, παθητὴν ὑπεισῆλθον σάρκα. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ εἶδον τὸ γένος τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἀπάτῃ καὶ οὐκ ἀνάγκῃ, γοητείᾳ δαιμόνων καὶ οὐ βίᾳ κρατούμενον, ὑπῆλθον τὸ ὑμέτερον σῶμα, ἵνα ἐκ τῶν ἐναντίων τὰ ἐναντία κατασκευάσας διὰ πάσης ἐξαπάτης ἐλευθερώσω τὸν ἄνθρωπον. Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ μέγα ἐφρόνει ὁ τύραννος, ὅτι τὴν ἁμαρ τίαν εὑρὼν καὶ διὰ τῆς ἁμαρτίας τὸν θάνατον εἰσαγαγὼν τὸν Ἀδὰμ τὸν τοῦ παραδείσου πολίτην, τὸν χειροτονητὸν τῆς οἰκου μένης δεσπότην, δοῦλον καὶ λῃστὴν καὶ γηπόνον ἐποίησεν, διὰ τοῦτο ἐπεχωρίασα τῇ γῇ ὡς βασιλεὺς τὴν σάρκα ὡς ἁλουργίδα ἔχων, ἵνα τοῦ τυράννου ἀποκείρας τὸ θράσος τῇ μὲν ἀπάτῃ τὴν ἀπάτην λύσω, τῇ δὲ ἁμαρτίᾳ τὴν δικαιοσύνην ἐπιστρατεύσω, τῷ δὲ θανάτῳ τὴν ζωὴν ἐπαφήσω. Οὐ φοβούμενος οὖν τὸν θάνατον δειλιῶ· οὐ γὰρ ἀκούσιον τὸ πρᾶγμα, ἀλλ' αὐτοπροαίρετον τὸ κατόρθωμα.
thought_title: The heretics' dilemma and Christ's answer
orientation: The heretics are still pressing their objection that Christ's prayer to avoid the cup proves he feared death, and Amphilochius now turns to Christ himself to answer them.
pass_a_gloss: it is in you either to accept or to refuse the passion. But if it does not lie in you, reasonably you fear as unwilling and against your will being dragged to the passion. But if unwillingly you take up the death on our behalf, how do you say: I have authority to lay down my soul and I have authority again to take it, and how again in another place mocking the threat of the Jews you were saying: Destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it? The one therefore who in many ways many times before death prefigured death and before the cross traced out the trophy of the cross, the one who said that the son of man must be handed over and crucified and buried and on the third day rise, why having come now under the cross do you refuse death? For if the son of man must be handed over, how do you say: If possible let this cup pass? And altogether if you were not willing to suffer, why did you put on the passible body? But if wearing a passible body you come to the passion, why are you grieved and distressed? And how when you were describing death, when you were narrating the passion, when you were prefiguring the cross, were you angry at Peter saying: Mercy to you, Lord, this shall never happen to you, and were you so angry as to say: Get behind me, Satan, you are a stumbling block to me, because you do not think the things of God but the things of men? If therefore it is a human thought to refuse death, for what reason do you now seek what long ago you were preventing? And how now do you pray to avoid death, you who long ago rebuked the disciple for fearing the assault of death? Are you not the one proclaimed beforehand by the law and the prophets? Did not Hosea the prophet say about you: Thus says the Lord: From the hand of Hades I will deliver them, so that they may say: Where is your victory, death, where is your sting, Hades? If therefore you are the one delivering from Hades, how do you fear death? But if you fear death, through which we hope to conquer death, vain is our hope, useless is our expectation. And altogether if you fear death, in what shall we have henceforth the hopes of life, and how do you say: I am the life and the resurrection? For life does not fear death, resurrection does not fear passion. But you are the life and the resurrection. Why then do you frighten my soul, why do you loosen the sinews of my mind by bringing forth words of fear? Was it a phantom, the things concerning Lazarus? Was it a dream, the things concerning the daughter of Jairus? Was it a shadow, the things concerning the son of the widow? But truth were the things that happened. How then does the one who stripped death fear death, and how does the one who raises the stinking dead with authority pray and fear to fall into death? And why altogether do you fear falling in? For even if you fall in, you will set free. For the one who raises others, much more raises his own body. Either tell me then the meaning, Master, or cease from the saying and do not tear apart my soul, or you will make my reasoning give way. For if you are the one knowing all things before their coming to be, how now do you not know whether it is possible or impossible for the cup to pass? For if you do not know, Paul lies saying that No creature is hidden before you, but all things are naked and laid open to his eyes. But if you know, how do you say: If possible? It is of one who does not know to ask, and not of one who knows to declare. Tell us then, Master, the meaning of the things said. For now Eunomius rejoices, now Arius is glad, seizing the word as a pretext for blasphemy. But in vain they rejoice. For there is no rejoicing for the impious, says the Lord. For I do not fear death, as they say; I do not refuse the passion, as they think. 2 For if I did not wish through death to grant life to the race of men, I would not, being the impassible Word, have entered into passible flesh. But since I saw the race of men held by deception and not by necessity, by sorcery of demons and not by force, I entered your body, so that having prepared the opposite things from the opposite things through every deception I might set free the man. For since the tyrant was thinking great things, because having found sin and through sin having brought in death he made Adam the citizen of paradise, the appointed master of the inhabited world, a slave and a robber and a tiller of the ground, for this reason I visited the earth as a king having the flesh as a purple robe, so that having shorn the tyrant's boldness by deception I might dissolve the deception, and against sin I might send righteousness as an ally, and against death I might let loose life. Not fearing therefore death do I fear; for the matter is not involuntary, but the achievement is self-chosen.

lemmas.gloss: I will send as an ally

choices.why: The verb is emphatic and first-person present; the gloss keeps the paradoxical force of Christ's statement that his fear is not fear of death.
The royal garment imagery is central to the kingly metaphor; 'purple robe' preserves the concrete image.
The shearing metaphor is vivid and concrete; keeping 'shorn' preserves the image of cutting away the tyrant's arrogance.

choices.english: I will send as an ally
choices.why: The verb means to march against or bring to bear as a military force; 'send as an ally' captures the strategic, martial sense against sin.
The noun denotes a successful deed or accomplishment; 'achievement' preserves the sense of a deliberate, praiseworthy act.

pass_b_english: it lies within your power either to accept the passion or to refuse it. But if it does not lie within you, then you fear with good reason, as one dragged to the passion unwillingly and against your will. And if you take up death for us unwillingly, how can you say, “I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again” (John 10:18)? And how, again, when you were mocking the threat of the Jews in another place, did you say, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19)? You who many times and in many ways prefigured death before death, and sketched the trophy of the cross before the cross—you who said that the Son of Man must be handed over and crucified and buried and rise on the third day—why do you now, when you have come under the cross, refuse death? For if the Son of Man must be handed over, how can you say, “If it is possible, let this cup pass”? And if you did not want to suffer at all, why did you put on a body capable of suffering? But if you put on a body capable of suffering and are going to the passion, why are you grieved and distressed? And how is it that when you were describing death, when you were narrating the passion, when you were prefiguring the cross, you were angry with Peter for saying, “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall never happen to you” (Matthew 16:22)—and you were so angry that you said, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, because you are not thinking the things of God but the things of men” (Matthew 16:23)? If refusing death is a human way of thinking, why do you now seek what you once prevented? And how do you now pray to escape death, you who once rebuked your disciple for fearing the assault of death? Are you not the one proclaimed beforehand by the law and the prophets? Was it not about you that the prophet Hosea said, “Thus says the Lord: I will deliver them from the hand of Hades, so that they may say, ‘Where is your victory, death? Where is your sting, Hades?’” (Hosea 13:14)? If you are the one who delivers from Hades, how do you fear death? And if you fear death—the death through which we hope to conquer death—then our hope is empty and our expectation is useless. If you fear death at all, in what shall we have hope of life from now on? And how can you say, “I am the life and the resurrection” (John 11:25)? For life does not fear death, and resurrection does not fear the passion. But you are the life and the resurrection. Why then do you frighten my soul? Why do you weaken the strength of my mind by bringing out words of fear? Were the things concerning Lazarus a phantom? Were the things concerning Jairus's daughter a dream? Were the things concerning the widow's son a shadow? No, what happened was truth. How then does the one who stripped death fear death? How does the one who raised stinking corpses with authority pray and fear to fall into death? And why do you fear falling into it at all? For even if you fall into it, you will free yourself. The one who raises others will far more raise his own body. So either explain the meaning to me, Master, or stop the saying and do not tear my soul apart or make my reasoning give way. For if you are the one who knows all things before they come into being, how do you now not know whether it is possible or impossible for the cup to pass? If you do not know, then Paul lies when he says, “No creature is hidden from your sight, but all things are naked and laid open to his eyes” (Hebrews 4:13). But if you do know, how can you say, “If it is possible”? A question belongs to one who does not know, not a statement to one who knows. So explain to us, Master, the meaning of what you have said. For now Eunomius rejoices; now Arius celebrates, seizing the saying as material for blasphemy. But they rejoice in vain. For there is no joy for the wicked, says the Lord (Isaiah 57:21). I do not fear death, as they say; I do not refuse the passion, as they suppose. For if I had not wanted to give life to the human race through death, I would not, being the impassible Word, have entered into flesh capable of suffering. But since I saw the human race held by deception and not by force, by the sorcery of demons and not by violence, I entered into your body, so that by preparing opposites from opposites I might set humanity free through every deception. For since the tyrant was boasting greatly that he had found sin and through sin brought in death, and had made Adam—the citizen of paradise, the appointed master of the world—a slave, a robber, and a tiller of the ground, for this reason I came to the earth as a king, having the flesh as a purple robe, so that having shorn the tyrant's boldness, I might dissolve deception with deception, march righteousness against sin, and set life against death. It is not because I fear death that I am afraid; for the matter is not involuntary, but the achievement is freely chosen.

problems.quote: "No creature is hidden from your sight, but all things are naked and laid open to his eyes" (Hebrews 4:13)
problems.source_quote: Οὐκ ἔστι κτίσις ἀφανὴς ἐνώπιόν σου, πάντα δὲ γυμνὰ καὶ τετραχηλισμένα τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς αὐτοῦ
problems.why: Source quotes Heb 4:13 with 'his eyes' (αὐτοῦ), but English says 'your sight' then 'his eyes', mixing persons.
problems.fix: "No creature is hidden from him, but all things are naked and laid open to his eyes" (Hebrews 4:13)
problems.ruling: Source has σου/αὐτοῦ consistent third person; English mixes 'your sight' with 'his eyes', obscuring reference.

problems.why: Middle voice: 'you will free yourself', not transitive 'set free' (no object). Christ frees himself.
problems.ruling: ἐλευθερώσῃ is future middle; 'you will set free' lacks reflexive force and implied object 'yourself' (ἑαυτόν).

problems.quote: send righteousness as an ally against sin
problems.source_quote: τῇ δὲ ἁμαρτίᾳ τὴν δικαιοσύνην ἐπιστρατεύσω
problems.why: ἐπιστρατεύσω means 'march against'/'make war upon'; righteousness attacks sin, not allies with it.
problems.ruling: 'ally against' misreads ἐπιστρατεύσω = 'campaign/march against'; righteousness attacks sin, not allied with it.

edits.old: "No creature is hidden from your sight, but all things are naked and laid open to his eyes" (Hebrews 4:13)
edits.new: "No creature is hidden from him, but all things are naked and laid open to his eyes" (Hebrews 4:13)

edits.old: send righteousness as an ally against sin

fixed: Fixed the mixed person in the Hebrews 4:13 quotation: source has 'αὐτοῦ' ('his eyes'), so changed 'your sight' to 'him'.
Fixed 'you will set free' to 'you will free yourself': source 'ἐλευθερώσῃ' is middle voice, meaning Christ frees himself.
Fixed 'send righteousness as an ally against sin' to 'march righteousness against sin': source 'ἐπιστρατεύσω' means to march against or make war upon, not to ally with.

problems.why: ὑπῆλθον means 'entered into' or 'took on,' not 'came under'; 'your body' should be 'your flesh/body' as assumption, not subordination.
problems.ruling: ὑπῆλθον means 'entered/undertook'; 'came under your body' wrongly implies subordination, changing theological meaning.

fixed: Mistranslation of 'ὑπῆλθον τὸ ὑμέτερον σῶμα': the verb means 'entered into' or 'took on,' not 'came under'; corrected to 'I entered into your body.'

last_rejected.source_quote: Οὐκ ἔστι κτίσις ἀφανὴς ἐνώπιόν σου, πάντα δὲ γυμνὰ καὶ τετραχηλισμένα τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς αὐτοῦ
last_rejected.why: The quotation is from Hebrews 4:13, but the text attributes it to Paul; the citation should not label it as Pauline.
last_rejected.ruling: Hebrews is traditionally attributed to Paul; citation format 'Paul says' plus '(Hebrews 4:13)' is standard convention, not error.

last_rejected.source_quote: Ὠσηὲ ὁ προφήτης ἔλεγεν· Τάδε λέγει κύριος· Ἐκ χειρὸς ᾅδου ῥύσομαι αὐτούς, ἵνα εἴπωσιν· Ποῦ ἡ νίκη σου, θάνατε, ποῦ τὸ κέντρον σου, ᾅδη;
last_rejected.why: The quotation matches 1 Corinthians 15:55, not Hosea 13:14 LXX; the source attributes it to Hosea but the wording is Paul's adaptation.
last_rejected.fix: Attribute as '(Hosea 13:14; cf. 1 Corinthians 15:55)' or similar, or cite as Pauline quotation.
last_rejected.ruling: Source says Ὠσηὲ ὁ προφήτης; English correctly attributes to Hosea. The wording question is a textual note, not a translation error.

last_rejected.quote: I might dissolve deception with deception
last_rejected.source_quote: τῇ μὲν ἀπάτῃ τὴν ἀπάτην λύσω
last_rejected.why: Christ's 'deception' is strategic bait, not mutual deception; 'dissolve deception by deception' misrepresents the soteriological strategy.
last_rejected.fix: I might undo deception by deception
last_rejected.ruling: τῇ ἀπάτῃ τὴν ἀπάτην λύσω literally means 'dissolve deception with deception'; translation accurately renders the Greek.

last_rejected.source_quote: τῷ δὲ θανάτῳ τὴν ζωὴν ἐπαφήσω
last_rejected.why: 'Set against' suggests opposition rather than application/attachment; ἐπαφίημι means to apply, let loose, or set upon.
last_rejected.fix: I might set life upon death
last_rejected.ruling: ἐπαφήσω with dative can mean 'set against'; 'set life against death' is within normal range and contextually appropriate.
